clues.title: Plate: red characters
text: Licence plates in Belgium use** red text**. You can recognise this distinct colour even through the blur.
clues.summary: Plates use red letters and numbers. You can spot the colour even through the blur.

clues.title: Bollard: white with yellow rectangle, or brown
text: Belgium uses **white** bollards with a **yellow rectangular reflector **on the front and [white ](https://goo.gl/maps/dsvrRBcicD5XmBN59)on the back. A second type of bollard is [dark brown](https://goo.gl/maps/Wefn7bM6gmvjQ7DY7) with two red stripes at the top. Occasionally, other bollards can be seen.
NOTE: Denmark uses similar white bollards, but they have a red stripe at the top and the reflector is not rectangular. The dark brown bollard with two red stripes can also be seen in the Netherlands.
clues.summary: A white bollard with a yellow rectangular reflector on the front, white on the back, or a dark brown one with two red stripes on top. The brown type also appears in the Netherlands.

differs.how: Danish white bollards have a red top stripe and a non-rectangular reflector

clues.title: Guardrail: A-type with yellow reflectors
text: Belgium uses A-type guardrails with **yellow **reflectors.

NOTE: In Europe, only Spain, Andorra, and Belgium use these reflectors. For a good overview of European guardrails, see [this infographic](https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/v1/60f6054f4e76b03092956de8/930bd2e7-57fa-4807-8e8a-733ba5a702a8/europeguardrail.png?format=2500w).
clues.summary: A-type guardrail with yellow reflectors. In Europe only Spain, Andorra and Belgium use yellow ones.

clues.title: Pole: square concrete, tiny holes, metal bands
text: Most poles in Belgium are concrete, square shaped, and have tiny holes running up them. They often have** small metal wrappings** around them. The second most common type of pole has [**oval-shaped holes**](https://goo.gl/maps/XVRAYg1wmhNJQxg17). You can find many different types of concrete poles in Belgium.
NOTE: The small metal wrappings can be found in France as well.
clues.summary: Square concrete poles with tiny holes running up them and small metal wrappings. The second most common type has oval holes. France has the metal wrappings too.

clues.title: Sign: blue or white direction signs
text: Directional signs in Belgium are most often blue or [white](https://goo.gl/maps/xWnWdzWmbcPDPTE4A).
clues.summary: Direction signs are most often blue or white.

clues.title: Sign: small extra blue plate under road signs
text: Road signs often have an additional **small blue sign**. In other European countries, these small signs are usually just white.

images.caption: A give way sign with a small blue plate under it; a white arrow points to the plate

clues.summary: Road signs often carry an extra small blue plate. Other European countries usually use white ones.

clues.title: Sign: crossing with two dotted lines
text: Belgium uses pedestrian crossing signs without any stripes, but with **two horizontal dotted lines**. The man on the sign has a **square head**.
NOTE: France and the Netherlands use a pedestrian sign with a regular zebra crossing with five vertical stripes.
clues.summary: The pedestrian crossing sign has no stripes, just two horizontal dotted lines, and the man has a square head. France and the Netherlands show a zebra crossing with five stripes.

differs.how: Sign shows a zebra crossing with five stripes
Sign shows a zebra crossing with five stripes

clues.title: Kilometre marker: green, sometimes red text
text: Kilometre markers in Belgium are often green, but can have [red text](https://goo.gl/maps/s18C6tj6L1qZXbVZ6) as well.
clues.summary: Kilometre markers are often green, and can have red text.

clues.title: Chevron: white with a red arrow
text: Belgium uses white chevrons, with a red arrow.
NOTE: The Netherlands also uses this chevron. You will not see these in France.
clues.summary: White chevrons with a red arrow. The Netherlands uses the same one, but France does not.

differs.how: France does not use this chevron

clues.title: Road: rural roads made of concrete slabs
text: A lot of rural roads in Belgium are made out of **concrete slabs**, almost like you would see in the Philippines or Thailand.
NOTE: The Netherlands almost never uses concrete slabs for roads.
clues.summary: Many country roads are made of concrete slabs, like in the Philippines or Thailand. The Netherlands almost never does this.

differs.how: Almost never has concrete slab roads

clues.title: Road lines: all white, bike lanes on both sides
text: Belgium uses all **white **road lines. These can be continuous or broken. Roads are often accompanied by** bike lanes** on both sides.
NOTE: Bikes and cycling lanes are most common in the Netherlands, but they can be often seen in Belgium as well.
clues.summary: All road lines are white, continuous or broken, and roads often have a bike lane on each side. This is even more common in the Netherlands.

clues.title: Houses: red brick
text: A lot of houses in Belgium are made of distinctive **red bricks**.
NOTE: This is more common in the North and West of the country.
clues.summary: Many houses are built of distinctive red brick, more so in the north and west.

clues.title: Houses: grey stone, French look
text: Houses in the South of the country use a lot of stone, have gray tones and generally look more French.
clues.summary: In the south, houses use a lot of stone, have grey tones and look more French.

clues.title: Signposts: orange posts and orange backs
text: Signposts in Belgium are often **orange**. The backs of signs are also sometimes orange. This is unique to Belgium.
clues.summary: Signposts are often orange, and the backs of signs are sometimes orange too. This is unique.

clues.title: Street sign: varied, short and tall
text: Street name signs in Belgium are very diverse, and often unique to a city. Most common colours are **white **and **dark** **blue**. They often have the** town or city name** written on them.
NOTE: These signs often have variable designs, but most of them are fairly short and tall. In comparison, Dutch street signs are almost always much longer than they are tall.
clues.summary: Street name signs vary a lot by city, mostly white or dark blue, and usually carry the town name. They are fairly short and tall, while Dutch ones are much longer than tall.

differs.how: Street signs are much longer than they are tall

clues.title: Sign: town entry white with black border
text: **Town entry signs** in Belgium are white with a black border. They also mention the name of the city or municipality in bold, black text.
clues.summary: Town entry signs are white with a black border and the town name in bold black text.

clues.title: Sign: small priority sign with orange diamond
text: Priority signs in Belgium have an **orange **diamond and are much **smaller **than in other countries.
clues.summary: The priority road sign has an orange diamond and is much smaller than elsewhere.

clues.title: Bus stop: yellow signposts and roofs
text: Bus stops are always marked by **yellow signposts**. Bus shelters often have **yellow roofs**.
clues.summary: Bus stops are always marked by yellow signposts, and bus shelters often have yellow roofs.

clues.title: Pole: striped traffic light poles
text: Traffic lights are most often supported by black-and-yellow or red-and-white **striped poles**.
NOTE: The regional differences are discussed in Step 2.

images.caption: Belgian traffic light pole painted in yellow and black stripes; the red arrow points at it

clues.summary: Traffic lights are mostly held by black-and-yellow or red-and-white striped poles. Which one you see depends on the region.

clues.title: Sign: red water hydrant sign with letter H
text: Belgium uses these **red** water hydrants signs with the letter **H **on top.
NOTE: You can also find these in Germany.
clues.summary: A red hydrant sign with the letter H on top. Germany has these too.

clues.title: Road: gutters on both sides
text: Almost all roads (big or small) in Belgium use **gutters **on both sides. This is much less common in neighbouring countries.

images.caption: Red circle and arrow mark the roadside gutter with a drain grate

clues.summary: Nearly all roads, big or small, have gutters on both sides. This is much rarer in neighbouring countries.

clues.title: Road lines: short dashed edges on bike paths
text: Belgian bicycle paths have short dashed outer lines.
clues.summary: Bicycle paths are edged with short dashed lines.

clues.title: Houses: many blurred
text: After Germany, Belgium is the next country in which you can find the most **blurred houses.**
clues.summary: Lots of houses are blurred. Only Germany has more blurred houses.

clues.title: Google car: red car with long antenna
text: Coverage with a** red car** and a **long antenna **can rarely be seen in Belgium.
NOTE: This is much more common in Ukraine.
clues.summary: A red car with a long antenna is rarely seen here. It is far more common in Ukraine.

clues.title: Coverage: low smallcam, wide round blur
text: Belgium also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front. The blur can also be fully transparent, making it harder to spot.
NOTE: Most of Western Europe also has smallcam.

images.caption: Four panels labelled front panned down, front panned straight, back panned down and good blur (front)

clues.summary: The newer Gen 4 smallcam sits lower than normal and has a big round blur with a small bump at the front. It can be see-through. Most of Western Europe has it.

clues.title: Landscape: flat northwest, hillier southeast
text: Belgium is generally **flat **in the northwest of the country, especially near the coast. The further [south east](https://goo.gl/maps/P9sjaiMA1DEcR4VY9) you go, the **hillier**.

images.caption: Landscapes compared: flat in the northwest (left) and hilly in the southeast (right)

clues.summary: Flat in the northwest, especially near the coast, and gets hillier the further southeast you go.

clues.title: Language: Dutch, French or German by region
text: Belgium has 3 official languages.
- **Dutch **(Flemish), spoken in **Flanders**, the Northern part of Belgium. There is an abundance of letters and combinations like z, w, ee and ij.
- **French **(Walloon), spoken in **Wallonia**, the Southern part of Belgium. You can see letters like ç, é, è and à.
- **German**, spoken in **Ostbelgien**, a small region in the east of the country. You can see letters like ä, ü, ö and ß.
clues.summary: Dutch in the north (lots of z, w, ee, ij), French in the south (ç, é, è, à), and German in a small eastern area (ä, ü, ö, ß).

clues.title: Sign: both French and Dutch on signs
text: Brussels, the capital of Belgium, is **bilingual**. You will see both French and Dutch on signs.

images.caption: A no-entry sign with a plate in French and Dutch below it

clues.summary: The capital is bilingual, so signs show both French and Dutch.

clues.title: Bus stop sign: white top or yellow top
text: Bus stop signs in Flanders (and Brussels) have a **white rectangle** at the top. In Wallonia they will have a [**yellow top**](https://goo.gl/maps/RXMysmC593bvR99HA).

images.caption: Bus stop signs with a white top (left) or a yellow top (right); red arrows link them to regions on the map

clues.summary: Bus stop signs have a white rectangle at the top in the north and in Brussels, and a yellow top in the south.

clues.title: Warning sign: thick red outline, no white edge
text: In Flanders (and Brussels), 95% of warning signs have a **thick red outline**, without a white border. Contrarily, you will most often find warning signs with a [**small white outline**](https://goo.gl/maps/UAv4N67VDRvvcSjJ7) in Wallonia.
NOTE: The signs found in Flanders are the same as the Spanish ones.

images.caption: Warning signs with a thick red outline and no white edge; red arrows link them to regions on the map

clues.summary: In the north and Brussels, 95% of warning signs have a thick red outline with no white border. In the south they usually have a thin white edge. The northern ones match Spain's.

clues.title: Pole: yellow-and-black traffic light poles
text: Traffic lights held up by **yellow-and-black** poles are unique to Flanders. In contrast, Wallonia and Brussels frequently use a **red-and-white** design.

images.caption: Traffic light pole painted in yellow and black stripes, boxed in white

clues.summary: Traffic lights on yellow-and-black poles are only found in the north. The south and Brussels often use red-and-white poles.

clues.title: Phone numbers: area code after the 0
text: Phone codes in Belgium are very useful to determine the region you are in. They are **9 **digits long. The 1 or 2 number(s) after the leading 0 indicate the area code.
0**X** XXX XX XX (Brussels, Antwerp, Liege, Ghent.)
0**XX** XX XX XX (Other cities.)
NOTE: Mobile numbers start with **04 **and are 10 digits long.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._
clues.summary: Numbers have 9 digits, and the one or two digits after the 0 give the area. Big cities use 0X XXX XX XX, other towns 0XX XX XX XX. Mobiles start with 04 and have 10 digits.

clues.title: Street sign: municipality name on the sign
text: As mentioned before, **municipality names** are often mentioned on street signs, usually in smaller font than the street name. The map shows a selection of recognizable street signs in the bigger cities.
NOTE: Of the big cities, **Bruges **(Brugge) is an exception to the rule of signs usually mentioning the municipality name.
_You can click on the image to enlarge it._
clues.summary: Street signs often show the municipality name in smaller type than the street. One big tourist city is an exception and usually leaves it out.

clues.title: Landscape: steep hills, dense forests, valleys
text: The Ardennes, located in the southeast part of Belgium, have a very distinct landscape. You can see a lot of **steep hills**, dense **forests, **and **valleys**.
NOTE: The Ardennes extend partially into France, Luxembourg, and Germany.
clues.summary: A hilly, wooded area with valleys in the southeast. The same hills continue into France, Luxembourg and Germany.

differs.how: Same hill range continues into Luxembourg
Same hill range continues into France
Same hill range continues into Germany

clues.title: Landscape: very flat polders with waterways
text: The coastal plain is extremely flat and consists of so-called **polders**, which are man-made fields at or below sea level, surrounded by many waterways. This landscape is situated near the North Sea coast, as well as near the western part of the border with the Netherlands, particularly around Antwerp.
NOTE: This part of Belgium is especially often confused with the Netherlands. Carefully look around for clues to distinguish the two countries if you find yourself in this landscape.
clues.summary: Extremely flat reclaimed fields at or below sea level, cut by many canals, near the North Sea and the western Netherlands border. Often confused with the Netherlands, so look for other clues.

differs.how: Very similar landscape, use signs or road lines

clues.title: Coast: wall of apartment blocks, dunes
text: Many parts of the Belgian **North Sea coast** are lined by apartment blocks, in a manner that is often derisively referred to as a “wall” of buildings by locals.
Near the coast, you will also sometimes be able to spot a [dune landscape](https://goo.gl/maps/oM2uuPVVeUfEZt839), with low bushes, long grass and sandy soil.
clues.summary: Much of the North Sea coast is lined with apartment blocks like a wall. You may also see dunes with low bushes and long grass.

clues.title: Border: small white crosses on the ground
text: Baarle-Hertog, located north-east of Antwerp, is composed of several exclaves and enclaves of Belgium and the Netherlands. You can often see the country's borders in this city (indicated by **small white crosses**). Street name signs tell you whether you are in Belgium or The Netherlands.

images.caption: Small white crosses on dark paving along a border

clues.summary: A town made of many mixed pieces of two countries shows small white crosses on the ground at borders. Street name signs tell you which country you are in.

differs.how: Street name signs show the Dutch side

clues.title: Language: Dutch with ij, ieuw, oe and straat
text: Dutch, often referred to as Flemish within Belgium, is a Germanic language. In Belgium, Dutch is spoken in the northern Flanders region, and alongside French in the capital city of Brussels.
Dutch features a lot of double vowels. Typical letter clusters are **ij, ieuw** and **oe**. “**IJ**“ written as one capitalised letter is also unique to the language.
The Dutch name for street is **straat**.
NOTE: Dutch is the main language of the Netherlands.

images.caption: Street sign reading Kruisstraat, Dutch for cross street

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Dutch has many double vowels and letter groups like ij, ieuw and oe. The word for street is straat. It is the main language of the north and shares Brussels with French.

differs.how: Same language, so use other clues

clues.title: Language: French with rue and accents
text: French is a Romance language closely related to languages like Catalan, Spanish and Italian. In Belgium, French is spoken in the southern Wallonia region, and alongside Dutch in the capital city of Brussels.
The French word for street is **rue**.
French uses these diacritics and special letters:
Accent aigu: **é**
Accent grave: **à, è, ù**
Accent circonflexe: **â, ê, î, ô, û**
Trema: **ë, ï, ü, ÿ**
Ligature: **œ**
Cédille: **ç** with a small hook
In addition, the **-ux** suffix is only found in French.
NOTE: French is also widely spoken in France, Luxembourg, Switzerland and Monaco.

images.caption: Blue street plate reading RUE DE SERPONT in French

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: French uses accents like é, à, è, â, ê, ç and the ending -ux. The word for street is rue. It is spoken in the south and, with Dutch, in Brussels.

differs.how: Same language, so use other clues
